front_question: List the 8 planets of our Solar System in increasing order of distance from the Sun.
back_answer:
1. Mercury (Smallest, closest)
2. Venus (Hottest, thick CO₂ atmosphere)
3. Earth (Water-rich, supports life)
4. Mars (Red Planet, iron oxide soil)
5. Jupiter (Largest gas giant)
6. Saturn (Prominent ring system)
7. Uranus (Ice giant rotating on side)
8. Neptune (Farthest cold ice giant).

• Mnemonic: 'My Very Energetic Mother Just Served Us Nuts.'

front_question: What is a Constellation? Give two prominent examples.
back_answer:
A constellation is an officially recognized group of stars forming a distinct pattern or figure in the night sky named after mythological characters, animals, or objects.
Examples: Saptarishi (Ursa Major / Big Dipper) and Orion (The Hunter).

front_question: How can you locate the Pole Star (Dhruva Tara) in the northern night sky using Saptarishi?
back_answer:
Locate the two outer 'pointer stars' on the bowl edge of the Saptarishi constellation. Extend an imaginary straight line upward through them; the line points directly to the fixed, bright Pole Star marking geographic North.

• Method: Celestial Pointer Star Alignment.
• Memory Trigger / Icon: 🌌↗️⭐ [Saptarishi Bowl Pointer Stars pointing to Polaris]

front_question: Why was Pluto reclassified as a 'Dwarf Planet' by the International Astronomical Union (IAU) in 2006?
back_answer:
Because Pluto shares its orbital path with numerous other icy Kuiper Belt objects and has not cleared its orbital neighborhood of celestial debris, violating IAU planet criteria 3.

• Concept Pair: Official Planet (Cleared Orbit) ↔ Dwarf Planet (Uncleared Orbit).

front_question: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun?
back_answer:
Venus possesses a dense, thick atmosphere composed of over 95% carbon dioxide gas, which creates an extreme runaway greenhouse heat trap that locks in solar thermal radiation.

• Cause: Runaway CO₂ Greenhouse Trap.

front_question: Distinguish between Stars, Planets, and Satellites.
back_answer:
• Stars: Huge, self-luminous celestial gas spheres generating light via nuclear reactions (e.g., Sun, Sirius).
• Planets: Non-luminous celestial bodies orbiting stars that shine by reflecting sunlight (e.g., Earth, Mars).
• Satellites: Natural or artificial bodies orbiting planets (e.g., Moon, INSAT).

• Memory Trigger / Icon: ⭐ [Star] | 🪐 [Planet] | 🛰️ [Satellite]
mnemonic_trigger: Memory Key: Connect observation to principle.

front_question: Where is the Hanle Dark Sky Reserve located and why is it ideal for astronomical telescopes?
back_answer:
Hanle is located in high-altitude desert cold region of Ladakh, India (~4,500 m elevation).
Ideal Features: Ultra-clear cloudless skies, low atmospheric water vapor, and zero urban light pollution.

• Historical Source: Indian Astronomical Observatory in Hanle, Ladakh.

front_question: Define 'Light Pollution' and its effect on stargazing.
back_answer:
Excessive, misdirected artificial outdoor lighting from city buildings and streetlights that brightens night sky background, washing out dim light from distant stars and galaxies.

• Memory Trigger / Icon: 🏙️💡 [City Streetlight Glow hiding Stars]
• Remedy: Dark Sky Reserves with shielded lighting.
mnemonic_trigger: Memory Key: Connect observation to principle.

front_question: Why does the Pole Star (Dhruva Tara) appear stationary in the northern sky while all other stars appear to revolve from East to West?
back_answer:
Because the Pole Star lies directly on the extended rotational rotational axis line of Earth above the geographic North Pole. As Earth rotates on its axis, Polaris remains fixed at the central axis point.

• Concept Pair: Axis Center (Stationary Polaris) ↔ Rotating Earth Surface (Moving Stars).
• Memory Trigger / Icon: 📌🌐 [Earth Rotational Axis pointing directly to Polaris]
mnemonic_trigger: Memory Key: Connect observation to principle.

front_question: How can a simple paper star chart (planisphere) or sky app be used during night stargazing?
back_answer:
Align star chart direction markers (N, S, E, W) with real compass directions. Hold chart overhead matching local time to identify visible constellations like Orion and Ursa Major.

front_question: Define 'Solar System' and state its central controlling body.
back_answer:
The gravitationally bound planetary system comprising the Sun at its center along with 8 planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and meteoroids.

• Central Mass: Sun contains 99.8% of total Solar System mass.

front_question: Why do sailors and desert nomads historically rely on the Pole Star for navigation?
back_answer:
Because the Pole Star permanently indicates true geographic North, allowing travelers to determine cardinal directions (N, S, E, W) at night without electronic equipment.

• Memory Trigger / Icon: ⛵🧭⭐ [Ship sailing North guided by Pole Star]

front_question: Why does the Moon show changing phases (New Moon to Full Moon) over a 29.5-day cycle?
back_answer:
As the Moon orbits Earth, the angle between Sun, Earth, and Moon changes continuously, altering the fraction of the Moon's sunlit hemisphere visible from Earth.

• Cycle: New Moon → Crescent → Quarter → Gibbous → Full Moon.

front_question: What is the difference between Asteroids and Comets?
back_answer:
• Asteroids: Rocky or metallic space bodies orbiting Sun mostly in Asteroid Belt between Mars and Jupiter.
• Comets: Icy snowballs of frozen gas, dust, and rock that develop glowing gas tails when approaching Sun.
